newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian sugar tariff to go despite revolt.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian sugar tariff to go despite revolt.

text.p: A revolt against the Australian government's decision to abolish tariffs on imported sugar was unlikely to stop the A$300 million market from being thrown open to competition from imports, industry analysts said.

Strong opposition to the Federal government's decision to abolish a A$55 a tonne tariff on imported raw and refined sugar has emerged from New South Wales (NSW), which produces only about five percent of Australia's annual sugar crop but which supplies about 25 percent of Australia's domestic market.
Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Tuesday that the Australian government would abolish the tariff on sugar imports from July 1 this year.
He also said that the government would retain the single-desk monopoly export sales system through the Queensland Sugar Corp.

Reluctant support by Queensland sugar cane growers for the tariff abolition has been based on what they see as a trade-off of the tariff abolition in return for retention of the export monopoly sales system.

"Even though the removal of the import tariff ... will adversely impact on the finances of individual growers, we accept (it is) the only way the sugar industry can satisfy National Competition Policy guidelines while retaining the core elements (of) single desk selling," Harry Bonanno, chairman of the CANEGROWERS organisation, said in a statement this week.

Opposition to ending the sugar tariff, which has simmered since the handing down of a report to the Sugar Industry Review Working Party last July recommending the tariff be dropped, emerged strongly in the wake of Howard's statement this week.

One National Party member of parliament (MP) has threatened to vote in parliament against the government on the tariff cut, another National Party MP has openly criticised the plan, while premiers of the states of NSW and Queensland spoke out against the plan.
The Federal government, a coalition of the Liberal Party and rural-based National Party, remains determined the tariff will be dropped.
"The decision remains," a spokesman for Primary Industries Minister John Anderson told Reuters on Thursday. He described opponents of abolition of the tariff as "local protectionists."
Asked if the tariff abolition was seen negotiable, Jim Simmons, general secretary of the NSW Cane Growers Association, said: "Not according to the Federal government".
Ian Ballantyne, general manager of Queensland grower organisation CANEGROWERS, also sees the government standing firm.
"If you had ten bucks I'd put it on it (being abolished)," he told Reuters.
Virtually all of NSW's sugar production is sold on Australia's domestic market, with the state supplying 20-25 percent of the nation's refined sugar needs.
The Queensland industry, which supplies 75-80 percent of the domestic market, sells only a minor proportion of its annual produce domestically.
Australia's domestic market for refined sugar has grown to almost 900,000 tonnes, with NSW supplying 220,000-250,000 tonnes.
Intense competition and price-cutting in the domestic Australian market for refined sugar in recent years had already brought domestic prices back to parity with world market prices, Simmons said.
Australia is officially forecast to produce a record 5.5 million tonnes of raw sugar in 1997/98, up from 5.3 million tonnes in 1996/97.
